Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery

Théo Saulus Affiliation: Mila - Quebec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal    Simon Lacoste-Julien Affiliation: Mila - Quebec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: Canada CIFAR AI Chair    Dhanya Sridhar Affiliation: Mila - Quebec AI Institute Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: Canada CIFAR AI Chair
Abstract

Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

1 Introduction

Complex systems can be described at different levels of abstraction: from low-level measurements about the system, one can form high-level summaries of its behavior. For example, we can record the neural activity of an individual performing a given task, and group the neurons by the stimuli they respond to, yielding a coarse description in terms of functional groups rather than individual neurons.

However, many scientific queries are about predicting the effects of interventions, such as "what happens if we activate this part of the brain?". Addressing such questions requires causal abstractions [Beckers and Halpern, 2019, Rubenstein et al., 2017]: put informally for now, a causal abstraction encodes at the high-level the effects of some interventions of interest on low-level variables, satisfying a form of consistency.

In mechanistic interpretability, this viewpoint motivates hypothesis testing methods where one proposes a candidate high-level model and checks whether it is implemented by a deep neural network (DNN) [Geiger et al., 2021, Geiger et al., 2024, Wu et al., 2023]. The underlying hope is that once we know the high-level computations the DNN implements, we can translate interventions on high-level variables into corresponding interventions on neurons to steer the model behavior. However, enumerating over candidate abstractions to test is costly, and worse, not possible when we study systems that we do not fully understand (for example, a DNN trained to solve protein folding). Motivated by these applications in interpretability and steering, this paper is about the unsupervised discovery of such causal abstractions.

Unsupervised objectives are typically under-specified and admit many equivalent solutions, thus requiring further constraints or assumptions. In this work, we discover causal abstractions for a family of low-level systems whose graphs exhibit a low-rank structure. Specifically, we consider factor directed acyclic graphs (factor DAGs, or f-DAGs), a family of models over low-level variables that are parameterized by a small number of latent factors, as introduced by Lopez et al. [2022]. This low-rank assumption is well-suited to modeling cell or neural biology where many low-level variables like genes or neurons carry out similar functions. Likewise in DNNs, because they perform computations in a distributed way, neurons are also likely to cluster into groups that capture the same abstract “concept” in a higher-level computation graph.

The goal of Lopez et al. [2022] was to learn a causal graph over low-level variables. They show that when observations come from a model that satisfies the f-DAG property, the DAG that best explains these low-level observations is likely to be unique and can be learned from data. Our goal with this paper is not to propose a new algorithm, but to prove that this causal discovery algorithm identifies a causal model over latent factors that is a causal abstraction of the low-level system. Additionally, we show that some assumptions allow us to make these latent factors identifiable up to trivial equivalence. We call this the anchor assumption. Loosely speaking, it requires that for each latent factor, there exist low-level variables that uniquely influence and are influenced by this factor. These anchor variables do not need to be known, but by ensuring that the solutions to Boolean matrix factorization satisfy the anchor assumption, we guarantee that the overall unsupervised objective only admits solutions that are simple reparameterizations of the true model over latent factors. We validate the theory empirically by studying simulated settings where the target causal abstraction is known, and also study a fully unsupervised case where we qualitatively analyze abstractions learned from a DNN that solves an arithmetic task.

2 Related work

Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level SCM preserves the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM through a state map and an intervention map [Rubenstein et al., 2017, Beckers and Halpern, 2019, Beckers et al., 2020]. This formalism has been used in mechanistic interpretability to test whether a proposed high-level causal model is implemented by a neural network [Geiger et al., 2021, Geiger et al., 2024, Geiger et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2023]. Our work instead studies the complementary problem of discovering such a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. This follows the older motivation of causal feature learning, which seeks macro-causes and macro-effects from high-dimensional observations [Chalupka et al., 2016, Chalupka et al., 2017], but uses the modern causal-abstraction formalism based on interventional consistency.

Several recent papers study learning causal abstractions rather than only testing expert-proposed ones. Zennaro et al. [2023], Felekis et al. [2024], Massidda et al. [2024], D’Acunto et al. [2025] learn abstraction maps between low- and high-level causal models, but they all require data or distributional information from both levels. In contrast, we discover the high-level latent SCM from low-level observations only. Zhu et al. [2024] are close to our work in their goal: they also consider unsupervised causal abstraction when the high-level variables are unknown. Their setting, however, relies on linear SCMs, shift interventions, linear state and intervention maps, and constructive abstractions, which implies that each low-level variable can only belong to one latent factor. In contrast, we identify high-level latent factors from low-level measurements through a low-rank hypothesis and weaker identifiability assumptions (the anchor condition). Targeted reduction of causal models [Kekić et al., 2024] learns a reduced high-level causal model and a map from low-level shift interventions to high-level interventions from interventional data. However, it is target-centered: the high-level model is built around a known variable of interest, rather than discovering a general latent-factor SCM.

Our structural assumptions connect causal abstraction discovery to low-rank causal discovery and latent-variable learning. We build on factor DAGs Lopez et al. [2022], where a low-rank adjacency structure is represented by latent factors mediating low-level causal relations. Low-rank causal discovery has also been studied as a structural restriction on causal graphs [Dong and Sebag, 2022, Fang et al., 2023]. Structural Causal Bottleneck Models [Bing et al., 2026], are closely related in that they posit that causal effects between high-dimensional variables can factor through low-dimensional bottlenecks, and they provide identifiability results for such bottlenecks. However, their framework treats bottlenecks primarily as task-specific sufficient summaries for estimating causal effects in a known graph, rather than as a learned high-level SCM equipped with explicit state and intervention maps satisfying a causal-abstraction criterion.

Our anchor assumption, inspired by topic modeling [Arora et al., 2012], can be related to pure-child assumptions in causal representation learning. For example, Xie et al. [2020] identify latent causal graphs in linear non-Gaussian measurement models using pure observed children of latent variables; Markham et al. [2023] introduce neuro-causal factor analysis, which learns latent common causes of observed measurements. These resemble our out-anchor condition, but our setting differs in that our observed variables also mediate latent factors relations. In different setups, other works about the identifiability of deep generative models [Moran et al., 2022, Lee and Gu, 2026] or about the identifiability of Boolean matrix factorization [Miron et al., 2021, DeSantis et al., 2022] also resort to very similar assumptions.

3 Background notions

In this section, we define structural causal models [Pearl, 2009] and introduce their properties before formalizing causal abstractions.

Definition 1 (Structural causal model).

A structural causal model (SCM) is a tuple ℳ=(𝒱,𝒰,ℱ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}), where:

  • •

    𝒱\mathcal{V} is a set of endogenous variables taking values in Val𝒱:=⋃V∈𝒱ValV\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{V}}:=\bigcup_{V\in\mathcal{V}}\mathrm{Val}_{V}. We denote by 𝐕⊂𝒱\mathbf{V}\subset\mathcal{V} a subset of these variables. Realizations of VV (respectively 𝐕\mathbf{V}) are denoted vv (resp. 𝐯\mathbf{v}).

  • •

    𝒰\mathcal{U} is a set of exogenous variables (or context), taking values in Val𝒰:=⋃U∈𝒰ValU\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}:=\bigcup_{U\in\mathcal{U}}\mathrm{Val}_{U}. We denote by 𝐔⊂𝒰\mathbf{U}\subset\mathcal{U} a subset of these variables. Realizations of UU (respectively 𝐔\mathbf{U}) are denoted uu (resp. 𝐮\mathbf{u}).

  • •

    for each V∈𝒱V\in\mathcal{V}, we define a mechanism FV∈ℱ:ValPaV×Val𝒰→ValV,F_{V}\in\mathcal{F}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{V}}\times\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{V}, where PaV⊆𝒱∖{V}\mathrm{Pa}_{V}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\setminus\{V\} is the set of endogenous parents of VV.

Crucially, SCMs provide a formalism for interventions.

Definition 2 (Intervention).

An intervention ii is described by a support 𝐈⊆𝒱\mathbf{I}\subseteq\mathcal{V} and a family of functions {IV}V∈𝐈\{I_{V}\}_{V\in\mathbf{I}} such that for each V∈𝐈V\in\mathbf{I}, IV:ValPaV×Val𝒰→ValVI_{V}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{V}}\times\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{V} replaces the original mechanism FVF_{V}. An intervention is hard if the functions IVI_{V} are constant assignments, which we denote i∈Hard𝐈i\in\mathrm{Hard}_{\mathbf{I}}. Otherwise, it is soft, which we denote i∈Soft𝐈i\in\mathrm{Soft}_{\mathbf{I}}.

Following Geiger et al. [2025], Eberhardt and Scheines [2007], we generalize the notion of soft interventions:

Definition 3 (Parametric interventions).

A parametric intervention ii is described by a support 𝐈⊆𝒱\mathbf{I}\subseteq\mathcal{V} and a family of functions {IV}V∈𝐈\{I_{V}\}_{V\in\mathbf{I}} such that for each V∈𝐈V\in\mathbf{I}, IV:SoftV→SoftVI_{V}:\mathrm{Soft}_{V}\to\mathrm{Soft}_{V} replaces the original mechanism FVF_{V} with IV​⟨FV⟩I_{V}\langle F_{V}\rangle. We denote i∈Para𝐈i\in\mathrm{Para}_{\mathbf{I}}.

In words, parametric interventions11 1 Called interventionals by Geiger et al. [2025]. depend on the original mechanisms of the SCM to perform their replacement. They extend the notion of soft interventions, which are simply “constant” parametric interventions. In the following, we denote ℐ\mathcal{I} the set of admissible interventions on ℳ\mathcal{M}, and we denote ℳi\mathcal{M}^{i} the SCM subject to the intervention i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}.

Given a context assignment 𝐮∈Val𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}, the SCM defines a system of equations ∀V∈𝒱,V=FV​(𝐯PaV,𝐮)\forall V\in\mathcal{V},\ V=F_{V}\bigl(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{V}},\mathbf{u}\bigr) whose solution (when it exists) is an endogenous assignment v∈ValVv\in\mathrm{Val}_{V}. We can use the graphical properties of an SCM to find its solutions [Halpern, 2000].

Definition 4 (Causal graph).

The causal graph of ℳ\mathcal{M} is the directed graph G=(𝒱,ℰ)G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) defined such that

(V1→V2)∈ℰ⇔V1∈PaV2(V_{1}\to V_{2})\in\mathcal{E}\quad\iff\quad V_{1}\in\mathrm{Pa}_{V_{2}}

The graph GG can be encoded by its adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×nA\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n} with Ai​j=1⇔(Vi→Vj)∈ℰA_{ij}=1\iff(V_{i}\to V_{j})\in\mathcal{E}.

Definition 5 (Solve\mathrm{Solve} operator).

For an intervention i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and a context 𝐮∈Val𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}} we denote by Solve⁡(ℳi,𝐮)∈Val𝒱\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}^{i};\mathbf{u})\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{V}} a solution to the system of equations defined by the SCM ℳi\mathcal{M}^{i}.

Assumption 1 (Strong acyclicity).

The causal graph of ℳ\mathcal{M} is independent of context 𝒰\mathcal{U}22 2 This notion is sometimes known as strong recursivity in the literature, e.g. in Beckers and Halpern [2019]..

In the setting we study, we will always assume strong acyclicity. Thus, we evaluate the mechanisms in topological order to find the unique solution to the Solve\mathrm{Solve} operator.

Finally, we can extend SCMs to the probabilistic case.

Definition 6 (Probabilistic causal models).

A probabilistic causal model is a tuple (ℳ,P​r)(\mathcal{M},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits) where ℳ\mathcal{M} is a SCM and P​r\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits is a probability distribution on contexts 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

In this setting, we consider the induced distribution on Solve⁡(ℳi,𝐮)\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}^{i};\mathbf{u}), following Beckers and Halpern [2019]:

P​rℳi⁡(𝐯):=P​r⁡({𝐮:Solve⁡(ℳi,𝐮)=𝐯})\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{M}^{i}}(\mathbf{v}):=\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits(\{\mathbf{u}:\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}^{i};\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{v}\})

Causal abstractions. A causal abstraction relates a low-level SCM ℒ=(𝒳,𝒰L,ℱL)\mathcal{L}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U}_{L},\mathcal{F}_{L}) and a high-level SCM ℋ=(𝒵,𝒰H,ℱH)\mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{U}_{H},\mathcal{F}_{H}) (typically containing much fewer variables), such that they both describe the same causal phenomena [Rubenstein et al., 2017].

Definition 7 (Exact transformations).

Let (ℒ,P​rL)(\mathcal{L},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{L}) and (ℋ,P​rH)(\mathcal{H},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{H}) be two probabilistic causal models. Let τ:Val𝒳→Val𝒵\tau:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{Z}} and ω:ℐL→ℐH\omega:\mathcal{I}_{L}\to\mathcal{I}_{H} be two partial surjective functions where ω\omega is order preserving.

(ℋ,P​rH)(\mathcal{H},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{H}) is an exact (τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-transformation of (ℒ,P​rL)(\mathcal{L},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{L}) if

∀i∈ℐL,P​rℋω⁡(i)=τ(P​rℒi),\forall i\in\mathcal{I}_{L},\quad\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{H}^{\omega(i)}}=\tau(\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{L}^{i}}),

where τ(P​rℒ)=P​rℒ({𝐱:τ(𝐱)=𝐳})\tau(\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{L}})=\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{L}}(\{\mathbf{x}:\tau(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{z}\}) denotes the pushforward distribution of P​rℒ\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{\mathcal{L}} by τ\tau.

Intuitively, for a causal abstraction to faithfully capture low-level effects at the high-level, applying ii at the low-level and translating outcomes via τ\tau matches applying ω⁡(i)\omega(i) directly at the high-level, which can be represented by the following commutative diagram:

We refer to τ\tau as the state map, and ω\omega as the intervention map.

Beckers and Halpern [2019] observe that the notion of exact transformation can be too weak because an unfortunate choice of P​rL,P​rH\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{L},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{H} may hide mechanistic mismatches. They therefore introduce uniform transformations:

Definition 8 (Uniform transformations).

ℋ\mathcal{H} is a uniform (τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-transformation of ℒ\mathcal{L} if for all distributions P​rL\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{L} on the low-level context 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L}, there exists a distribution P​rH\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{H} such that (ℋ,P​rH)(\mathcal{H},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{H}) is an exact (τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-transformation of (ℒ,P​rL)(\mathcal{L},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits_{L}).

4 Towards causal abstractions discovery

Most current applications of causal abstractions are related to neural network interpretability: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model ℋ\mathcal{H} about what logic the model might implement to solve a given task, and then tests whether the computational graph ℒ\mathcal{L} of a neural network implements it [Geiger et al., 2021, Geiger et al., 2024, Wu et al., 2023].

Intuitively, we view ℋ\mathcal{H} as a model of latents that summarize the computations done by the low-level computational graph ℒ\mathcal{L}: the value of each latent Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} can be computed with a subset of variables 𝐗⊆𝒳\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathcal{X}, and in turn there is another subset of variables 𝐗′⊆𝒳\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{X} which can essentially be determined by the value of this ZZ. In other words, ZZ summarizes all there is to know about the causal relations 𝐗→𝐗′\mathbf{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{X}^{\prime}.

Proposing a candidate high-level model ℋ\mathcal{H} is difficult, because it requires intuition or expertise about the task at hand: for instance, we can propose a logic for two-digit addition because we master this task. In the following, we develop assumptions under which we can learn a high-level model ℋ\mathcal{H} directly from low-level measurements by minimizing a differentiable objective.

In particular, we recall from Lopez et al. [2022] that for an SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} whose graph GG is low-rank, one can naturally construct a latent SCM ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{*}. We prove that this latent SCM ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{*} is a uniform transformation of ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since causal discovery tools allow us to learn the graph and mechanisms of ℳ\mathcal{M} from data, we propose later a practical algorithm for unsupervised causal abstraction discovery inspired by it.

Factor directed acyclic graphs. Consider the causal graph GG between observed variables 𝒳\mathcal{X}, encoded by an adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×nA\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}, where nn is the number of variables. In causal discovery, where we seek to learn the causal graph GG from observations, a common structural assumption to restrict the space of candidate graphs is the low-rankness of the adjacency matrix AA [Dong and Sebag, 2022, Fang et al., 2023]. More specifically, assuming that AA has Boolean rank m<nm<n means that there exists Q,R∈{0,1}n×mQ,R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m} such that

A=Q⋄R⊤:=⋁k=1m(Q∗k∧R∗k),A\ =\ Q\diamond R^{\top}\ :=\ \bigvee_{k=1}^{m}\bigl(Q_{*k}\wedge R_{*k}\bigr),

where ⋄\diamond denotes the Boolean matrix product, illustrated in Figure 2. Intuitively, this low-rank decomposition captures the idea that many low-level variables, like genes in a regulatory network [Alizadeh et al., 2000] or neurons in the brain [Yeo et al., 2011], share the same parents and children due to higher-order functions. Matrix factorization methods have previously been used to discover such higher-level functions [Newman et al., 2015].

This factorization admits a graphical interpretation via factor directed graphs.

Definition 9 (Factor SCM).

An f-SCM is an SCM ℳ=(𝒱,𝒰,ℱ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}) such that 𝒱\mathcal{V} is partitioned into two subsets: observed variables 𝒳={X1,…,Xn}\mathcal{X}=\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\} and unobserved latent factors 𝒵={Z1,…,Zm}\mathcal{Z}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}\}. Additionally, we suppose that the causal graph GG of an f-SCM is bipartite, directed, and strongly acyclic, and we denote it an f-DAG.

In particular, the edges in GG may only link variables to factors or factors to variables:

G=(𝒱=𝒳∪𝒵,ℰ𝒱),ℰ𝒱⊂(𝒳×𝒵)∪(𝒵×𝒳).G=(\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{X}\cup\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{V}}),\quad\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{V}}\subset(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z})\cup(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{X}).

Relating back to Boolean matrix factorization, the matrix QQ captures the adjacency matrix of directed edges from low-level variables to factors, i.e., 𝐗→𝐙\mathbf{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}, while RR captures the directed edges from factors 𝐙\mathbf{Z} back to low-level variables 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Thus, QQ and RR fully characterize the f-DAG.

Further, the graph GG can be collapsed into two distinct (“mono-partite”) graphs: one over variables GXG_{X} with

Xi→Xj⇔∃Z∈𝒵,Xi→Z→Xj​ in G,X_{i}\to X_{j}\iff\exists Z\in\mathcal{Z},\ X_{i}\to Z\to X_{j}\text{ in $G$,}

and one over factors GZG_{Z} defined analogously.

From now on, we will distinguish 3 different notions of parents in an f-DAG: for any Z∈𝒵,X∈𝒳Z\in\mathcal{Z},\ X\in\mathcal{X},

X′∈PaZ\displaystyle X^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z} ⇔X′→Z​ in ​G\displaystyle\iff X^{\prime}\rightarrow Z\text{ in }G
Z′∈PaX\displaystyle Z^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}_{X} ⇔Z′→X​ in ​G\displaystyle\iff Z^{\prime}\rightarrow X\text{ in }G
X′∈PaXL\displaystyle X^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}^{L}_{X} ⇔X′→X​ in ​GL\displaystyle\iff X^{\prime}\rightarrow X\text{ in }G_{L}
Z′∈PaZH\displaystyle Z^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}^{H}_{Z} ⇔Z′→Z​ in ​GH\displaystyle\iff Z^{\prime}\rightarrow Z\text{ in }G_{H}

Key idea. The notion of f-DAGs seems to meet our intuitive desiderata for causal abstractions discovery in that they summarize the way low-level variables interact with fewer factors, and they are learnable from data with low-rank causal discovery.

The following sections formalize these two points: we show how the factor-level description can indeed be cast as a uniform transformation of the variable-level description, and we identify conditions under which the factor representation is identifiable.

5 Theoretical results

This section formalizes the previous insights with three results that justify the use of low-rank causal discovery to discover causal abstractions: (i) first, we show that if we knew the underlying f-SCM that generates low-level observations, we could derive a causal abstraction of the low-level model; (ii) since we do not know the underlying f-SCM, we establish assumptions under which Boolean matrix factorization can recover the latent factor variables up to simple reparameterizations; (iii) completing the story, we derive assumptions under which the full high-level SCM can be recovered up to simple reparameterizations. We state our main results, and sketch some of the proofs; the full derivations are available in Appendix B.

5.1 f-SCMs build causal abstractions

Let ℳ=(𝒳∪𝒵,𝒰,ℱ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{X}\cup\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}) be an f-SCM. Denote GG the associated f-DAG, and denote GLG_{L} (resp. GHG_{H}) its collapse on the observed variables 𝒳\mathcal{X} (resp. latent factors 𝒵\mathcal{Z}). Furthermore, suppose that there is no direct link from exogenous variables 𝒰\mathcal{U} to latent factors 𝒵\mathcal{Z}: intuitively, we think of factors as summarizing low-level measurements, and we may not want to consider that this summary stochastic. In other words, ℳ\mathcal{M} admits the following mechanisms:

∀X∈𝒳,FX:ValPaX×Val𝒰→ValX\displaystyle\forall X\in\mathcal{X},\ F_{X}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}}\times\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{X}
∀Z∈𝒵,FZ:ValPaZ→ValZ\displaystyle\forall Z\in\mathcal{Z},\ F_{Z}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{Z}

where PaX⊆𝒵\mathrm{Pa}_{X}\subseteq\mathcal{Z} and PaZ⊆𝒳\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{X}.

These mechanisms imply the following low-level mechanisms over ℒ=(𝒳,𝒰,ℱL)\mathcal{L}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}_{L}) and high-level mechanisms over ℋ=(𝒵,𝒰,ℱH)\mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}_{H}) when collapsing on either type of node (see Figure 1 for an illustration):

FXL:ValPaXL×Val𝒰→ValX𝐱,𝐮↦FX​({FZ​(𝐱PaZ)}Z∈PaX,𝐮)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} F^{L}_{X}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}^{L}_{X}}\times\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}&\to\mathrm{Val}_{X}\\ \mathbf{x},\mathbf{u}&\mapsto F_{X}\Big(\{F_{Z}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}})\}_{Z\in\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u}\Big)\\ \end{aligned}
FZH:ValPaZH×Val𝒰→ValZ𝐳,𝐮↦FZ​({FX​(𝐳PaX,𝐮)}X∈PaZ)\displaystyle\begin{aligned} F^{H}_{Z}:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathrm{Pa}^{H}_{Z}}\times\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}&\to\mathrm{Val}_{Z}\\ \mathbf{z},\mathbf{u}&\mapsto F_{Z}\Big(\{F_{X}(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u})\}_{X\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}\Big)\\ \end{aligned}

where PaXL=⋃Z∈PaXPaZ⊆𝒳\mathrm{Pa}_{X}^{L}=\bigcup_{Z\in\mathrm{Pa}_{X}}\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}\subseteq\mathcal{X} and PaZH=⋃X∈PaZPaX⊆𝒵\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}^{H}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}\mathrm{Pa}_{X}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}. That is, we compose together how low-level variables define factors and how those factors define downstream low-level variables. Note that ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℋ\mathcal{H} share here the same context 𝒰\mathcal{U}, coming from the f-SCM ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Example 1.

As a concrete example, based on Figure 1, the mechanism FZ3HF^{H}_{Z_{3}} for the high-level variable Z3Z_{3} in the collapsed model ℋ\mathcal{H} is a function of Z1Z_{1} to Z2Z_{2} such that FZ3H=FZ3​(FX4​(Z1),FX6​(Z2))F^{H}_{Z_{3}}=F_{Z_{3}}(F_{X_{4}}(Z_{1}),\ F_{X_{6}}(Z_{2})).

Key idea. The first result is to show that if we knew the f-SCM that generates observations of low-level variables, the corresponding collapsed SCM ℋ\mathcal{H} over the factors alone is a valid causal abstraction of the collapsed SCM ℒ\mathcal{L} over low-level variables alone. To derive this result, we will show that ℋ\mathcal{H} is an exact transformation of ℒ\mathcal{L}. To show this property, we will first need to define all the relevant mappings from low-level to high-level.

Intervention sets. We consider ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} to be a subset of all possible hard interventions Hard𝒳\mathrm{Hard}_{\mathcal{X}}, and ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H} a subset of parametric interventions Para𝒵\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal{Z}} that we characterize below.

State map. The state map τ:Val𝒳→Val𝒵\tau:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{Z}} reconstructs factors from variables using the underlying mechanisms ℱ\mathcal{F}:

∀𝐱∈Val𝒳,∀Z∈𝒵,(τ⁡(𝐱))Z=FZ​((𝐱)PaZ).\displaystyle\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{X}},\ \forall Z\in\mathcal{Z},\quad(\tau(\mathbf{x}))_{Z}=F_{Z}((\mathbf{x})_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}).

Intervention map. The intervention map ω\omega translates hard interventions on 𝒳\mathcal{X} to parametric ones on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}:

ω:ℐL⊆Hard𝒳\displaystyle\omega\ :\ \mathcal{I}_{L}\subseteq\mathrm{Hard}_{\mathcal{X}} →ℐH⊆Para𝒵\displaystyle\to\mathcal{I}_{H}\subseteq\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal{Z}}
iL\displaystyle i_{L} ↦iH\displaystyle\mapsto i_{H}

More specifically, iL∈ℐLi_{L}\in\mathcal{I}_{L} is a hard intervention characterized by its support 𝐈L⊆𝒳\mathbf{I}_{L}\subseteq\mathcal{X} and the replacement of some low-level mechanisms by some constant assignment:

∀X∈𝐈L,FXL​(⋅)←CX∈ValX\forall X\in\mathbf{I}_{L},\ F_{X}^{L}(\cdot)\leftarrow C_{X}\in\mathrm{Val}_{X}

In the corresponding high-level system, iH∈ℐHi_{H}\in\mathcal{I}_{H} is a parametric intervention characterized by its support

𝐈H:=⋃X∈𝐈LChX\mathbf{I}_{H}:=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{I}_{L}}\mathrm{Ch}_{X}

and the replacement of some high-level mechanisms: ∀Z∈𝐈H,FZH←IZH​⟨FZH⟩\forall Z\in\mathbf{I}_{H},\ F_{Z}^{H}\leftarrow I_{Z}^{H}\langle F_{Z}^{H}\rangle, where for any 𝐳∈Val𝒵\mathbf{z}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{Z}} and 𝐮∈Val𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}},

IZH​⟨FZH⟩​(𝐳PaZH,𝐮):=FZ​({FX∗​(𝐳PaX,𝐮)}X∈PaZ)\displaystyle I_{Z}^{H}\langle F_{Z}^{H}\rangle(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}^{H}},\mathbf{u}):=F_{Z}\Big(\{F^{*}_{X}(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u})\}_{X\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}\Big)

where FX∗={CXX∈𝐈LFXX∉𝐈LF_{X}^{*}=\begin{cases}C_{X}&X\in\mathbf{I}_{L}\\ F_{X}&X\notin\mathbf{I}_{L}\end{cases}.

Example 2.

Continuing the previous example, a hard intervention i∈ℐL:X4←C4i\in\mathcal{I}_{L}:X_{4}\leftarrow C_{4} will modify FZ3HF^{H}_{Z_{3}} by replacing it with FZ3H=FZ3​(C4,FX6​(Z2))F^{H}_{Z_{3}}=F_{Z_{3}}(C_{4},\ F_{X_{6}}(Z_{2})).

In words, ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H} contains the parametric interventions that are realizable given the current underlying mechanisms ℱ\mathcal{F} and all hard interventions ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} allowed in 𝒳\mathcal{X}33 3 A careful reader will see that our definition of ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} considers that low-level hard interventions only disconnect edges Z→XZ\to X from the perspective of the f-SCM ℳ\mathcal{M}, not X→ZX\to Z ones..

Theorem 1 (Uniform transformation).

With τ\tau and ω\omega defined as above, ℋ\mathcal{H} is a uniform (τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-transformation of ℒ\mathcal{L}.

The proof, available in Appendix B.1, essentially verifies the points of Definition 7 and 8 one by one. The commutativity of the diagram is proven by induction, from root to leaf nodes, and relies importantly on the fact that context is shared between ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℒ\mathcal{L}.

5.2 Identifiability of the f-DAG

Factors 𝒵\mathcal{Z} are unobserved latents, hence the question of whether they are recoverable from data. Indeed, without further assumptions, one could imagine splitting a given factor ZZ into two factors without affecting any observed variable. First, we focus on the graphical structure and study the identifiability of the adjacency matrix AA and of its factorization Q⋄R⊤Q\diamond R^{\top} up to simple reparameterizations.

Assumption 2.

The low-level SCM ℒ\mathcal{L} verifies causal sufficiency, Markov property, and faithfulness44 4 These assumptions are required for the identifiability statements, but not for Theorem 1..

Assumption 3.

Each factor Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} has at least two parents in GG.

Under Assumption 2 and 3, Lopez et al. [2022] show that the low-rank assumption on the adjacency matrix AA over variables 𝒳\mathcal{X} reduces the Markov equivalence class (MEC) over the graph GLG_{L}, thus making it often identifiable.

Lemma 1 (Identifiability of GLG_{L}, from Lopez et al. [2022]).

Under Assumption 3, the MEC of GLG_{L} reduces to a singleton.

Starting from this point, we propose conditions to ensure that the full f-DAG GG, including the latent factors, is identifiable up to permutation of indices. We present identifiability results for the mechanisms in the next section.

The key extra assumption we introduce involves the existence of “anchors” for each latent factor. In topic modeling, anchors are words that are specific to a given topic: they only belong to one cluster, and no other [Arora et al., 2012]. Inspired by this idea, we define anchors for factors.

Definition 10 (Anchors).

For X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} and Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z}, we say that XX is an in-anchor of ZZ if ChX={Z}\mathrm{Ch}_{X}=\{Z\}, i.e., the only child of XX is ZZ in GG. Analogously, XX is an out-anchor of ZZ if PaX={Z}\mathrm{Pa}_{X}=\{Z\}, i.e., the only parent of XX is ZZ in GG.

In matrix terms, this means that for any factor ZZ with index kk, XX is an in-anchor of ZZ if its index ii is such that Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1 and ∀l≠k,Qi​l=0\forall l\neq k,Q_{il}=0, i.e., the sum (in ℕ\mathbb{N}) of the row ii is 1 exactly. We can interpret out-anchors similarly on RR.

Assumption 4.

Each factor Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} has at least one in-anchor and one out-anchor.

In high dimensional systems, Assumption 4 is fairly reasonable: canonical marker genes are genes that may uniquely identify a given cell type [Zeisel et al., 2015], and some regions of the brain correspond to “specialized functional components” [Sporns and Betzel, 2016] where it is reasonable that some neurons in these specialized regions are anchors for the whole region. Similarly, when solving some task, some neurons of a large neural network may only contribute to one high-level concept, while most of them contribute to many.

In particular, this assumption is softer than other causal abstraction frameworks which usually assume constructive abstractions, which implies that 𝒳\mathcal{X} can be partitioned into cells [Chalupka et al., 2016, Geiger et al., 2021], i.e., all parents of a latent ZZ are in-anchors, and all its children are out-anchors.

Fix an adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×nA\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n} with rank⁡(A)=m≤n\mathrm{rank}(A)=m\leq n55 5 The Boolean rank of AA is not easy to compute if one had to do it in practice, it is NP-complete [Orlin, 1977], but is uniquely defined by only looking at AA.. By definition of the Boolean rank, there exists a decomposition of mm terms A=Q⋄R⊤A=Q\diamond R^{\top} with Q,R∈{0,1}n×mQ,R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m}.

Lemma 2 (Reading Q,RQ,R in AA).

Under Assumption 4, the columns of QQ and the rows of R⊤R^{\top} are readable in AA.

Intuitively, an anchor connects to exactly one latent factor, so its row/column in AA directly copies that factor’s connectivity pattern. For two vectors x,y∈ℝnx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we write x≤yx\leq y if ∀i∈[n],xi≤yi\forall i\in[n],x_{i}\leq y_{i}.

Definition 11 (Minimality).

A row Ai∗A_{i*} is minimal if it is not null, and there is no other non-zero row Ah∗A_{h*} such that Ah∗≤Ai∗A_{h*}\leq A_{i*} and Ah∗≠Ai∗A_{h*}\neq A_{i*}. Minimal columns are defined analogously.

This notion depends only on AA, and characterizes the rows for which no other row is a strict subset of them.

Lemma 3 (Minimality-anchor correspondence).

Under Assumption 4, in-anchors correspond to the minimal rows of AA, and out-anchors to the minimal columns of AA.

Anchors appear as the minimal rows and columns in the adjacency matrix because their pure connection patterns cannot be formed by combining the connections of other factors.

Theorem 2 (Identifiability of (Q,R)(Q,R)).

Under Assumption 4, a Boolean factorization A=⋁k=1mQ∗kRk∗⊤A=\bigvee_{k=1}^{m}Q_{*k}R_{k*}^{\top} is unique up to a simultaneous permutation of the mm factors.

Recovering the correct causal graph identifies the connections drawn by the latent factors, but does not give access to their actual values. The next section exposes what additional equivalence classes f-SCMs are subject to.

5.3 Identifiability of the mechanisms

Latent factors are only observed through their downstream effect on the variables, so the mechanisms of an f-SCM are identifiable only up to some reparameterization of the factor value spaces. This section makes this statement precise and gives simple conditions under which the admissible reparameterizations reduce to affine or monotone transformations.

Definition 12 (𝒳\mathcal{X}-equivalence).

Two f-SCMs ℳ,ℳ~\mathcal{M},\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} are 𝒳\mathcal{X}-equivalent if they induce the same low-level collapsed mechanisms on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, i.e., ∀X∈𝒳,FXL=F~XL\forall X\in\mathcal{X},\ F_{X}^{L}=\widetilde{F}_{X}^{L}.

Lemma 4 (Reparameterization symmetry).

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an f-SCM and let (ρZ)Z∈𝒵(\rho_{Z})_{Z\in\mathcal{Z}} be any family of bijections ρZ:ValZ→ValZ\rho_{Z}:\mathrm{Val}_{Z}\to\mathrm{Val}_{Z}. Define ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} over the same f-DAG by F~Z:=ρZ−1∘FZ\widetilde{F}_{Z}:=\rho_{Z}^{-1}\circ F_{Z} and F~X​(𝐳PaX,𝐮):=FX​((ρZ​(𝐳Z))Z∈PaX,𝐮)\widetilde{F}_{X}\bigl(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u}\bigr):=F_{X}\bigl((\rho_{Z}(\mathbf{z}_{Z}))_{Z\in\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u}\bigr). Then ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} is 𝒳\mathcal{X}-equivalent to ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Factors can be reparameterized by arbitrary bijections without affecting observational and interventional behavior on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We propose assumptions to restrict this equivalence class.

Definition 13 (Linear parent mechanisms).

An f-SCM has linear parent mechanisms if for every Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} the mechanism FZF_{Z} is affine: for all 𝐱∈Val𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{X}},

FZ​(𝐱PaZ)=bZ+∑X∈PaZaZ​X​𝐱X,F_{Z}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}})=b_{Z}+\sum_{X\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}}a_{ZX}\mathbf{x}_{X},

where aZ​X,bZ∈ℝa_{ZX},b_{Z}\in\mathbb{R}, and with at least one nonzero coefficient per factor: ∀Z∈𝒵,∃X∈PaZ,aZ​X≠0\forall Z\in\mathcal{Z},\ \exists X\in\mathrm{Pa}_{Z},\ a_{ZX}\neq 0.

Theorem 3 (Linear parent identifiability).

Let ℳ,ℳ~\mathcal{M},\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} be two 𝒳\mathcal{X}-equivalent f-SCMs sharing the same f-DAG with out-anchors for all factors, linear parent mechanisms and real supports. Then for every Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} there exists a unique bijection ρZ\rho_{Z} such that F~Z=ρZ−1∘FZ\tilde{F}_{Z}=\rho_{Z}^{-1}\circ F_{Z}, and it is affine: ρZ:𝐳Z↦αZ​𝐳Z+βZ\rho_{Z}:\mathbf{z}_{Z}\mapsto\alpha_{Z}\mathbf{z}_{Z}+\beta_{Z} with αZ≠0\alpha_{Z}\neq 0

We show in Appendix B.5 similar results when child mechanisms are affine.

These results motivate the metrics that should be used to evaluate the method in practice. In particular, using metrics invariant to linear reparameterization to match factors ZZ against external hypotheses only makes sense if we are willing to assume linearity of the mechanisms.

6 Practical implementation

We now specify the learning objective for our unsupervised causal abstraction discovery method (UCAD), and show additional connections with causal abstractions. Our practical implementation draws inspiration from low-rank causal discovery, with specific additional constraints. On synthetic experiments, we show that our algorithm recovers ground-truth latent factors, up to the expected equivalence classes predicted by theory.

6.1 Learning objective

We extend the low-rank causal discovery objective of Lopez et al. [2022] with specific additional constraints. We parameterize separately the conditional distributions with Θ\Theta and the causal graph with Φ\Phi. The constrained optimization problem is the following:

maxΦ,Θ⁡S⁡(Φ,Θ)​ such that ​{𝒞DAG​(Φ)=0𝒞anchors​(Φ)=0𝒞sparsity​(Φ)≤tols\displaystyle\max_{\Phi,\Theta}S(\Phi,\Theta)\text{ such that }\begin{cases}\mathcal{C}^{\text{DAG}}(\Phi)=0\\ \mathcal{C}^{\text{anchors}}(\Phi)=0\\ \mathcal{C}^{\text{sparsity}}(\Phi)\leq\text{tol}_{s}\end{cases}

Objective function.

S⁡(Φ,Θ)=𝔼G′∼G⁡(Φ)i∼ℙ​𝔼𝐱∼pdata(i)​∑X∉𝐈log⁡pΘX​(𝐱X∣𝐱PaXG′)\displaystyle S(\Phi,\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}G^{\prime}\sim G(\Phi)\\ i\sim\mathbb{P}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p^{(i)}_{\text{data}}}\sum_{X\notin\mathbf{I}}\log p_{\Theta}^{X}(\mathbf{x}_{X}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}^{G^{\prime}}})

with G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi) the causal graph model, ℙ\mathbb{P} is the empirical distribution over intervention regimes ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L}, pdata(i)p^{(i)}_{\text{data}} the empirical distribution over observed variables 𝒳\mathcal{X} under intervention ii, and pΘXp_{\Theta}^{X} is a density model for the conditional distribution of X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} conditioned on its parents PaXG′\mathrm{Pa}_{X}^{G^{\prime}} in the sampled graph G′∼G⁡(Φ)G^{\prime}\sim G(\Phi).

Our graph model G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi) is parametrized with a Gumbel-softmax on a matrix W∈{−1,0,1}n×mW\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n\times m} such that Qi​j=𝟏{Wi​j=1}Q_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{W_{ij}=1\} and Ri​j=𝟏{Wi​j=−1}R_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{W_{ij}=-1\}. This way, Qi​jQ_{ij} and Ri​jR_{ij} cannot be simultaneously equal to 11, and no self-loop is introduced.

Our conditional densities pΘXp_{\Theta}^{X}, which aim to recover the mechanisms FXLF_{X}^{L}, are parameterized such that for each factor ZZ indexed by k∈[m]k\in[m] in QQ and each variable XX indexed by j∈[n]j\in[n] in RR, we have:

𝐳Z=FZΘ(Q:k𝐱);𝐱X∼Normal(FXΘ(Rj:𝐳),σj2)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{Z}=F_{Z}^{\Theta}(Q_{:k}\mathbf{x});\qquad\mathbf{x}_{X}\sim\text{Normal}(F_{X}^{\Theta}(R_{j:}\mathbf{z}),\ \sigma_{j}^{2})

where σj2>0\sigma_{j}^{2}>0, and FZΘ,FXΘF_{Z}^{\Theta},F_{X}^{\Theta} are linear models or MLP in practice. In other words, we assume additive Gaussian noise on variables, while we do not introduce noise on factors.

Acyclicity constraint. 𝒞DAG\mathcal{C}^{\text{DAG}} enforces that the final graph is indeed a DAG. Several formulations have been proposed in the literature, which we describe in Appendix C. Additionally, we propose a constraint formulation for the case where variables X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} are “layered”, as in a neural network where a neuron X1X_{1} cannot causally influence another neuron X2X_{2} if both are in the same layer or if X2X_{2} precedes X1X_{1} in the computational graph. In other words, we restrict the search space to block upper-triangular adjacency matrices. For a low-rank matrix A=Q⋄R⊤A=Q\diamond R^{\top}, this translates into the per-factor condition:

∀k∈[m],maxi:Qi​k=1ℓ(i)<minj:Rj​k=1ℓ(j),\forall k\in[m],\qquad\max_{i:Q_{ik}=1}\ell(i)<\min_{j:R_{jk}=1}\ell(j),

i.e., every parent selected by column Q:kQ_{:k} lies in a strictly earlier layer than every child selected by column R:kR_{:k}. This translates into a differentiable constraint that can be efficiently computed in O⁡(n​m+m​L)O(nm+mL) time, with LL the number of layers, applied on G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi):

𝒞DAG(Φ):=∑klp≥lc[∑i:ℓ⁡(i)=lpQ(Φ)i​k][∑j:ℓ⁡(j)=lcR(Φ)j​k]\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\text{DAG}}(\Phi):=\sum_{\underset{l_{p}\geq l_{c}}{k}}\left[\sum_{i:\ell(i)=l_{p}}Q(\Phi)_{ik}\right]\left[\sum_{j:\ell(j)=l_{c}}R(\Phi)_{jk}\right]

Anchor constraint. As discussed previously, the Boolean factorization of the adjacency matrix is not unique unless additional assumptions are made, e.g. Assumption 4. For our model to find such solutions, we consider 𝒞anchor\mathcal{C}^{\text{anchor}}, applied to G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi).

A factor ZZ indexed by k∈[m]k\in[m] has an in-anchor if and only if there exists a row i∈[n]i\in[n] such that Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1 and ∀ℓ≠k:Qi​ℓ=0\forall\,\ell\neq k:Q_{i\ell}=0. Equivalently,

∀k∈[m],maxi⁡Qi​k​⋀ℓ≠k(1−Qi​ℓ)=1\forall k\in[m],\quad\max_{i}Q_{ik}\bigwedge_{\ell\neq k}(1-Q_{i\ell})=1

We have a similar formulation for out-anchors. This formulation is made differentiable using classic optimization tricks, to finally obtain 𝒞anchor\mathcal{C}^{\text{anchor}}, as described in Appendix C.

Sparsity constraint

As in many causal discovery algorithms, we impose some sparsity constraint on the learned graph, in the form of an L1L_{1} constraint

𝒞sparsity​(Φ):=∑i​j|Q​(Φ)i​j|+|R​(Φ)i​j|m​n\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\text{sparsity}}(\Phi):=\frac{\sum_{ij}|Q(\Phi)_{ij}|+|R(\Phi)_{ij}|}{mn}

One can adjust the tolerance level tols\text{tol}_{s} depending on prior knowledge of the structure to be learned.

6.2 Link with causal abstractions

Exact transformation is a binary notion, while it is intuitive to have a gradient in how close ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℋ\mathcal{H} are. Following Beckers et al. [2020], we introduce a soft notion that captures this intuition:

Definition 14 (Approximate transformation).

Let (ℒ,P​r)(\mathcal{L},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits) and (ℋ,P​r)(\mathcal{H},\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits) be two probabilistic causal models sharing their context 𝒰\mathcal{U}. Let τ:Val𝒳→Val𝒵\tau:\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{Z}} and ω:ℐL→ℐH\omega:\mathcal{I}_{L}\to\mathcal{I}_{H} be two partial surjective functions where ω\omega is order preserving.

Let dHd_{H} a distance on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, ℙ\mathbb{P} a probability distribution over ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L}, and η≥0\eta\geq 0 a scalar. ℋ\mathcal{H} is a η\eta-(τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-approximate transformation of ℒ\mathcal{L} if

𝔼i∼ℙ𝐮∼P​r​[dH​(τ⁡(Solve⁡(ℒi,𝐮)),Solve⁡(ℋω⁡(i),𝐮))]≤η\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\sim\mathbb{P}\\ \mathbf{u}\sim\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits\end{subarray}}\left[d_{H}\left(\tau\big(\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{L}^{i};\mathbf{u})\big),\mathrm{Solve}\big(\mathcal{H}^{\omega(i)};\mathbf{u}\big)\right)\right]\leq\eta

Note that other choices of statistics than 𝔼\mathbb{E} can be made depending on the use-case, and that we specialized the definition to match our case where 𝒰\mathcal{U} is shared by ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℋ\mathcal{H}. Taking η=0\eta=0 recovers the definition of exact transformation.

In practice, τ^,ω^\hat{\tau},\hat{\omega}, and ℋΦ,Θ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi,\Theta} are learned, and we wish that

Δ^:=𝔼i∼ℙ𝐮∼P​r​[dH​(τ^​(Solve⁡(ℒi,𝐮)),Solve⁡(ℋΦ,Θω^​(i),𝐮))]\hat{\Delta}:=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\sim\mathbb{P}\\ \mathbf{u}\sim\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits\end{subarray}}\left[d_{H}\left(\hat{\tau}\big(\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{L}^{i};\mathbf{u})\big),\mathrm{Solve}\big(\mathcal{H}^{\hat{\omega}(i)}_{\Phi,\Theta};\mathbf{u}\big)\right)\right]

diminishes as the model is trained.

Theorem 4 (Approximate transformation bound).

If all mechanisms FZΘ,FXΘF_{Z}^{\Theta},F_{X}^{\Theta} are Lipschitz, then Δ^\hat{\Delta} is linearly bounded by S⁡(Φ,Θ)S(\Phi,\Theta).

In words, under regularity conditions on the learned mechanisms, the learned high-level model ℋΦ,Θ\mathcal{H}_{\Phi,\Theta} is an η\eta-(τ^−ω^)(\hat{\tau}-\hat{\omega})-approximate transformation of the ground-truth low-level model ℒ\mathcal{L}, and η\eta diminishes as a linear function of the learning objective diminishes.

6.3 Practical implementation

We implement66 6 See https://github.com/theosaulus/ucad. this constrained optimization problem using PyTorch [Ansel et al., 2024] and Cooper [Gallego-Posada et al., 2025].

6.4 Empirical results

Synthetic. We validate UCAD on synthetic f-SCMs with setups ranging from linear noiseless mechanisms with layered structure to nonlinear mechanisms with Gaussian noise on variables XX on non-layered DAGs. In all settings, ground-truth f-DAGs are generated with enforced anchors and models are trained on a mix of observational and interventional regimes. See Appendix D for details.

For each setup, we generate 55 DAGs, on which we train 6060 UCAD models with varying hyperparameters and seed. For each DAG, we select the configuration with lowest validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) among those that reached constraint feasibility.

Since we aim to assess the recovery of latent factors, we pay particular attention to the mean correlation coefficient (MCC), which finds the alignment with highest absolute Pearson correlation between the learned and ground-truth factors. When dealing with arbitrary non-linear transformations, we consider MCC-RDC, which is based on the randomized dependence coefficient [Lopez-Paz et al., 2013]. Both metrics are invariant to permutation of the latents.

In the case where we expect the f-SCM to be recoverable up to linear reparametrization (i.e., when FXF_{X} and/or FZF_{Z} are affine), a perfect MCC-Pearson of 11 is theoretically attainable. The performance of our model is fairly invariant to the number of variables (16,6416,64 or 128128) and factors (3,63,6 or 88), to whether the DAG has a layered structure or not, and to whether additive Gaussian noise is added on the variables. When averaging over all these cases (13 experiments) we measure an average MCC (Pearson) of 0.830.83. Importantly, the variability we observe between cases does not seem to depend on whether both FX,FZF_{X},F_{Z} are linear or only one.

We report MCC for a set of experiments in Table 1. In addition, we report MCC after applying random orthogonal transformations to both ground-truth factors and learned factors, to contextualize the results. MCC is equal to 11 when the latent factors are perfectly recovered, up to linear reparametrization and permutation of indices, and decreases when the factors are mixed. This comparison shows that our method recovers latents that are not only related to the ground-truth factors, but are also aligned with their coordinates.

In the case where both FX,FZF_{X},F_{Z} are non-linear, theory predicts that can only recover the factors up to an arbitrary bijective transformation, which results in a drop of MCC-Pearson (0.630.63). The MCC-RDC score remains high, at 0.790.79 in the 64 variables case, and 0.700.70 in the 16 variables case.

These experiments tend to indicate that when assumptions are satisfied, it is possible to train a model that is capable to recover the ground truth factors, following theory. We still note a significant variability between each example, both in terms of performance and in which hyperparameters end up reaching the lowest validation NLL; algorithmic improvements and better search may help future developments.

Neural network interpretability. To test UCAD on a real DNN, we consider the problem of divisibility by 6. Solving this problem is intuitively performed by checking divisibility by 2 (by looking at the last digit) and by 3 (by checking whether the sum of all digits is divisible by 3, recursively).

Let the input be n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\dots,N\} represented in base 1010 as (d0,…,dK−1)∈{0,…,9}K(d_{0},\dots,d_{K-1})\in\{0,\dots,9\}^{K}, and let the output be y=𝟏​[6∣n]∈{0,1}y=\mathbf{1}[6\mid n]\in\{0,1\}. We consider the concepts:

c2=𝟏​[2∣n],c3=𝟏​[3∣n],c6=c2∧c3.\displaystyle c_{2}=\mathbf{1}[2\mid n],\qquad c_{3}=\mathbf{1}[3\mid n],\qquad c_{6}=c_{2}\wedge c_{3}.

To match the intuitive process of computing c3c_{3}, we also consider an alternative concept c~3=∑kdk\tilde{c}_{3}=\sum_{k}d_{k}. This problem possesses natural “negative controls” that are irrelevant: divisibility by an unrelated prime (e.g. 5,7,115,7,11).

We train five MLPs with 33 hidden layers of size 3232 to solve this task for digits between 0 and 1 million, until convergence. Then, we gather the 9696 activations for unseen numbers and train our UCAD model with 33 factors and report reconstruction metrics in Table 2.

We measure a stronger reconstruction of hypothesized concepts than with negative controls (average MCC-RDC of 0.720.72 vs. 0.070.07 over 5 experiments). In particular, one of the factors has an average Pearson correlation of 0.800.80 with c2c_{2}, which is a strong signal that it is consistently implemented by the network. Reasonably high MCC-RDC coefficients can be observed for c6c_{6} and c3c_{3} (0.550.55 and 0.320.32), especially compared to negative controls which are not reconstructed as well (at most 0.140.14). These results remain difficult to interpret, because a low agreement with some concept could sometimes be an indication that the DNN implements a different strategy to solve the problem, for example a heuristic that works only up to 1 million.

7 Discussion and future work

In this paper, we demonstrated that it is possible to discover causal abstractions directly from low-level measurements without relying on an expert to propose a candidate high-level model. By leveraging factor directed acyclic graphs and introducing the anchor assumption, we proved that low-rank causal discovery methods can identify high-level latent factors up to simple reparameterization. We translated these theoretical guarantees into a practical learning objective and empirically tested it on both synthetic datasets and a small neural network.

While our theoretical results provide a foundation for UCAD, they rely on knowing the true number of latent factors. A direction for future work is understanding the behavior of the learning objective when this number is misspecified.

Scaling our approach to larger and more complex systems is another direction. Our current experiments on the divisibility task highlight the difficulty of interpreting the heuristics learned by deep neural networks. Applying it to larger models in language, vision, or to noisy scientific data, will require finding scalable optimization procedures.

In particular, the hope of a causal abstraction in mechanistic interpretability lies in its ability to reliably control a system’s output. Future research should focus on steering experiments, to test whether intervening on the unsupervised discovered high-level factors can reliably alter the behavior of DNNs on complex tasks.

  • •

    for each X∈𝐈LX\in\mathbf{I}_{L} a constant assignment CXC_{X} by which FXF_{X} is replaced.

We therefore define the following partial order relation over ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H}:

Lemma 5 (Partial order on ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H}).

Lemma 6.

ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} and ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H} can be equipped with partial orders ⪯L\preceq_{L} and ⪯H\preceq_{H}, and ω\omega is order preserving with respect to them.

Proof.

Let’s address each point.

Defining ⪯L\preceq_{L}

We choose what is often referred to as the “natural” partial order [Beckers and Halpern, 2019]: for a,b∈ℐLa,b\in\mathcal{I}_{L},

a⪯Lb⇔{𝐈La⊆𝐈Lb∀X∈𝐈La,CXa=CXb\displaystyle a\preceq_{L}b\iff\begin{cases}\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\subseteq\mathbf{I}^{b}_{L}\\ \forall X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L},\ C^{a}_{X}=C^{b}_{X}\end{cases}

Defining ⪯H\preceq_{H}

We choose ⪯H\preceq_{H} as introduced in Lemma 5.

ω\omega is order preserving

Let a,b∈ℐLa,b\in\mathcal{I}_{L} such that a⪯Lba\preceq_{L}b. In other words, we have: 𝐈La⊆𝐈Lb\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\subseteq\mathbf{I}^{b}_{L} and ∀X∈𝐈La,CXa=CXb\forall X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L},\ C^{a}_{X}=C^{b}_{X}

For all Z∈𝐈Hω⁡(a)=⋃X∈𝐈LaChXZ\in\mathbf{I}_{H}^{\omega(a)}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}}\mathrm{Ch}_{X}, the intervention ω⁡(a)\omega(a) sets the internal mechanisms FXF_{X} to a CXC_{X} for all X∈𝐈La∩PaZX\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\cap\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}.

Since 𝐈La⊆𝐈Lb\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\subseteq\mathbf{I}^{b}_{L}, we obtain:

𝐈Hω⁡(a)=⋃X∈𝐈La⊆⋃X∈𝐈Lb=𝐈Hω⁡(b)\displaystyle\mathbf{I}_{H}^{\omega(a)}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}}\subseteq\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{I}^{b}_{L}}=\mathbf{I}_{H}^{\omega(b)}

Additionally, we get:

∀Z∈𝐈Hω⁡(a),𝐈La∩PaZ⊆𝐈Lb∩PaZ\displaystyle\forall Z\in\mathbf{I}^{\omega(a)}_{H},\quad\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\cap\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{I}^{b}_{L}\cap\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}

Then, since we have ∀X∈𝐈La,CXa=CXb\forall X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L},\ C^{a}_{X}=C^{b}_{X}, we get:

∀Z∈𝐈Hω⁡(a),∀X∈𝐈La∩PaZ,CXa=CXb\displaystyle\forall Z\in\mathbf{I}^{\omega(a)}_{H},\ \forall X\in\mathbf{I}^{a}_{L}\cap\mathrm{Pa}_{Z},\quad C^{a}_{X}=C^{b}_{X}

Putting things together:

Theorem 1 (Uniform transformation).

With τ\tau and ω\omega defined above, ℋ\mathcal{H} is a uniform (τ−ω)(\tau-\omega)-transformation of ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Proof.

We verify one by one the points of Definition 7.

Basic properties

ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} and ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H} are sets of interventions, and (ℐL,⪯L)(\mathcal{I}_{L},\preceq_{L}) and (ℐH,⪯H)(\mathcal{I}_{H},\preceq_{H}) define partially ordered sets, by Lemma 6.

GLG_{L} and GHG_{H} are acyclic, so ℒi\mathcal{L}^{i} and ℋω⁡(i)\mathcal{H}^{\omega(i)} have unique solutions under the Solve\mathrm{Solve} operator for a given context 𝐮∈Val𝒰\mathbf{u}\in\mathrm{Val}_{\mathcal{U}}.

τ\tau is surjective if we restrict its codomain to its image on the solution of ℒ\mathcal{L} under ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L}.

ω\omega is surjective: by construction, ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H} contains exactly the high-level parametric interventions induced by the allowed low-level hard interventions in ℒ\mathcal{L}.

ω\omega is order preserving by Lemma 6.

B.2 Discussion on the ordering of interventions

When we apply two interventions i1,i2i_{1},i_{2} on ℳ\mathcal{M}, it might occur that some variables are affected by both i1i_{1} and i2i_{2}. To determine which assignment prevails, Geiger et al. [2025] introduce the notion of intervention algebras, to fix the order in which the interventions are applied:

Definition 15 (Intervention algebras).

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be a set of interventions allowed on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. We equip it with an associative composition operator ∘:ℐ×ℐ→ℐ\circ:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{I} and an identity element id\mathrm{id}. The pair (ℐ,∘)(\mathcal{I},\circ), together with id\mathrm{id}, forms an intervention algebra if the following properties are verified:

  • •

    the identity element id\mathrm{id} is defined such that ℳi​d=ℳ\mathcal{M}^{id}=\mathcal{M}, i.e., no intervention performed.

  • •

    the composition operator ∘\circ is such that ∀i1,i2∈ℐ,ℳi1∘i2=(ℳi1)i2\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in\mathcal{I},\ \mathcal{M}^{\,i_{1}\circ i_{2}}=(\mathcal{M}^{\,i_{1}})^{\,i_{2}}, and ∘\circ is commutative if i1i_{1} and i2i_{2} target different variables, and left-annihilative if they target the same:

    (i1∘i2)V={(i2)Vif ​V∈𝐈2(i1)Vif ​V∈𝐈1∖𝐈2(id)Vif ​V∉𝐈1∪𝐈2\displaystyle(i_{1}\circ i_{2})_{V}=\begin{cases}(i_{2})_{V}&\text{if }V\in\mathbf{I}_{2}\\ (i_{1})_{V}&\text{if }V\in\mathbf{I}_{1}\setminus\mathbf{I}_{2}\\ (\mathrm{id})_{V}&\text{if }V\notin\mathbf{I}_{1}\cup\mathbf{I}_{2}\end{cases}

An induced partial order ⪯\preceq is defined by ∘\circ such that ∀i1,i2∈ℐ,i1⪯i2⇔i2∘i1=i2\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in\mathcal{I},\ i_{1}\preceq i_{2}\iff i_{2}\circ i_{1}=i_{2}, i.e., the model ℳi2∘i1\mathcal{M}^{i_{2}\circ i_{1}} remains identical to ℳi2\mathcal{M}^{i_{2}} if and only if i1i_{1} agrees with the replacements performed by i2i_{2}.

As shown by Geiger et al. [2025], hard and soft interventions both can always be equipped with an intervention algebra. This is not the case of parametric interventions, which require more care.

Although the family of parametric intervention we consider might be relatable to intervention algebras, we stay closer to prior notions of exact transformation [Beckers and Halpern, 2019, Rubenstein et al., 2017] which only require the existence of partial orderings on ℐL,ℐH\mathcal{I}_{L},\mathcal{I}_{H} with respect to which ω\omega is order preserving.

B.3 Proof of Theorem 2

Lemma 1 (Identifiability of GLG_{L}, adapted from Lopez et al. [2022], Appendix B.2).

If every factor Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} has at least two parents in GG, then the MEC of GLG_{L} reduces to a singleton.

Proof.

Let (Xi,XjX_{i},X_{j}) be an unoriented edge in the essential graph of GLG_{L}. By definition of f-DAGs, there exists a factor Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} such that (Xi,Z)(X_{i},Z) and (Z,Xj)(Z,X_{j}) are part of GG. Because the edge is unoriented, it cannot be part of a v-structure in GLG_{L}.

In the case that every factor Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} has at least two parents, there can be no unoriented edges, and therefore the graph is identifiable. ∎

Recall Definition 10 and Assumption 4. Fix an adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×nA\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n} with rank⁡(A)=m≤n\mathrm{rank}(A)=m\leq n

For all Q,R∈{0,1}n×mQ,R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m} verifying Assumption 4, we have rank⁡(Q⋄R⊤)=m\mathrm{rank}(Q\diamond R^{\top})=m.

Let’s denote for this proof A~:=Q⋄R⊤=⋁k=1mQ∗k∧Rk∗⊤\widetilde{A}:=Q\diamond R^{\top}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{m}Q_{*k}\wedge R_{k*}^{\top}. This implies that A~ik​jk=1\widetilde{A}_{i_{k}j_{k}}=1, and A~ik​jℓ=0\widetilde{A}_{i_{k}j_{\ell}}=0 for k≠ℓk\neq\ell, because Qik​l=0Q_{i_{k}l}=0 for l≠kl\neq k and Rl​jℓ=0R_{lj_{\ell}}=0 for l≠ℓl\neq\ell by the anchor conditions.

Consider any rank-1 term q​r⊤qr^{\top} used in a factorization of A~\widetilde{A}. For the sake of contradiction, assume that it covers both entries (ik,jk)(i_{k},j_{k}) and (iℓ,jℓ)(i_{\ell},j_{\ell}) for k≠ℓk\neq\ell, i.e., qik=qiℓ=1q_{i_{k}}=q_{i_{\ell}}=1 and rjk=rjℓ=1r_{j_{k}}=r_{j_{\ell}}=1. Finally, rank⁡(A~)=m\mathrm{rank}(\widetilde{A})=m. ∎

A=𝟏3×3−I3=[011101110]A=\mathbf{1}_{3\times 3}-I_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&1\\ 1&0&1\\ 1&1&0\end{bmatrix}

Interestingly, we note that our assumption shares similarities with assumptions made in the Boolean matrix factorization literature. In particular, DeSantis et al. [2022] obtain a characterization of the notion of “free rank” that can be related to anchors, and Miron et al. [2021] derive a sufficient condition for the uniqueness of the factorization expressed in terms of vector support that also reminds of anchors. More connections could potentially be drawn to obtain more general results.

B.4 Towards a more flexible identifiability result

We introduce a more flexible condition that does not require that each factor has a in- and out-anchor. We only show a property of this condition, not a full identifiability result.

Definition 16 (rr-disjunctedness).

Columns of QQ are rr-disjunct if

∀k∈[m],∀S⊆[m]\{k}with|S|≤r,∃j∈[n]such thatQj​k=1and∀l∈S,Qj​l=0\displaystyle\forall k\in[m],\forall S\subseteq[m]\backslash\{k\}\quad\text{with}\quad|S|\leq r,\ \exists j\in[n]\quad\text{such that}\quad Q_{jk}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\forall l\in S,\ Q_{jl}=0

In words, every factor can be distinguished from the union of any combination of at most rr other factors by at least one parent variable.

Example: the following matrix is 1-disjunct but not 2-disjunct:

[1011110111100111]\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1&1\\ 1&1&0&1\\ 1&1&1&0\\ 0&1&1&1\\ \end{bmatrix}

Indeed, for any k≠lk\neq l, the column j=l+1mod4j=l+1\mod 4 satisfies Q12=0Q_{12}=0 and Qk​j=1Q_{kj}=1. 22-disjunctness fails because every column of QQ contains exactly one zero, so no column vanishes on two distinct rows simultaneously. Hence for any kk and any pair S={a,b}⊆[m]∖{k}S=\{a,b\}\subseteq[m]\setminus\{k\}, no column jj satisfies Qk​j=1Q_{kj}=1 and Qa​j=Qb​j=0Q_{aj}=Q_{bj}=0.

We can of course have a similar definition for the rows of R⊤R^{\top}. Note that considering r=m−1r=m-1 defines exactly the in-/out-anchors.

Definition 17 (Row and column sparsity).

The row-sparsity of QQ is denoted s⁡(Q)=max⁡∑ki⁡Qi​ks(Q)=\max_{i}\sum_{k}Q_{ik}, and similar definition for the column-sparsity of R⊤R^{\top}.

Lemma 9 (Reading Q,RQ,R from AA).

Let’s assume the following points:

  • •

    each factor ZZ has an in-anchor (resp. out-anchor)

    the columns of RR (resp. QQ) are rr-disjunct

  • •

    m−1≥r≥s⁡(Q)m-1\geq r\geq s(Q) (resp. s⁡(R)s(R))

Then (Q,R)(Q,R) can be read in AA.

Proof.

Recovering RR. For all factors ZZ with index kk there exists an in-anchor XX with index ii, i.e. Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1 and ∀l≠k,Qi​l=0\forall l\neq k,Q_{il}=0. We can thus read the values of RR directly in AA (see above).

Ai∗A_{i*} is the ∨\vee of the rows of RR. For all variable index i∈[n]i\in[n], let’s define Gi={k:Qi​k=1}G_{i}=\{k:Q_{ik}=1\}. By definition, |Gi|≤s⁡(Q)|G_{i}|\leq s(Q). We have the following:

Ai​j=⋁l=1m(Qi​l∧Rl​j)=⋁k∈Gi(1∧Rk​j)=⋁k∈GiRk​jA_{ij}=\bigvee_{l=1}^{m}(Q_{il}\wedge R_{lj})=\bigvee_{k\in G_{i}}(1\wedge R_{kj})=\bigvee_{k\in G_{i}}R_{kj}

Written with row notations:

Ai∗=⋁k∈GiRk∗A_{i*}=\bigvee_{k\in G_{i}}R_{k*}

Uniqueness. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that this ∨\vee-decomposition is not unique. Then there exists T≠ST\neq S such that |S|,|T|≤R|S|,|T|\leq R and Ai∗=⋁l∈SRl∗=⋁l∈TRl∗A_{i*}=\bigvee_{l\in S}R_{l*}=\bigvee_{l\in T}R_{l*}. Pick h∈S\Th\in S\backslash T. By rr-disjunctness on the set TT, there exists j∈[n]j\in[n] such that Rh​j=1R_{hj}=1 and ∀l∈T,Rl​j=0\forall l\in T,R_{lj}=0. In particular, we have ⋁l∈TRl​j=0\bigvee_{l\in T}R_{lj}=0. Therefore we have at the same time ⋁l∈TRl​j=0\bigvee_{l\in T}R_{lj}=0 and ⋁l∈SRl​j=1\bigvee_{l\in S}R_{lj}=1, and thus ⋁l∈SRl∗≠⋁l∈TRl∗\bigvee_{l\in S}R_{l*}\neq\bigvee_{l\in T}R_{l*}. This is contradictory with the hypothesis we made, so the set GG is the unique ∨\vee-decomposition of size at most rr.

Recovering QQ with SS. Let’s prove that ∀i∈[n],∀k∈[m],Qi​k=1⇔Rk∗≤Ai∗\forall i\in[n],\forall k\in[m],Q_{ik}=1\iff R_{k*}\leq A_{i*}

  • •

    If Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1, then k∈Gik\in G_{i}, and Ai∗=⋁l∈GiRl∗A_{i*}=\bigvee_{l\in G_{i}}R_{l*} so in particular Rk∗≤Ai∗R_{k*}\leq A_{i*}

  • •

    If Rk∗≤Ai∗R_{k*}\leq A_{i*}, let’s suppose for sake of contradiction that Qi​k=0Q_{ik}=0, which implies k∉Gik\notin G_{i}. By hypothesis, we have Rk∗≤Ai∗=⋁l∈GiRl∗R_{k*}\leq A_{i*}=\bigvee_{l\in G_{i}}R_{l*} with |Gi|≤R|G_{i}|\leq R. So there exists no jj such that Rk​j≥⋁l∈GiRl​jR_{kj}\geq\bigvee_{l\in G_{i}}R_{lj}, which contradicts the rr-disjunctedness. Therefore, Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1.

Finally, we have shown that there is a unique possibility for each entry of QQ, knowing A,RA,R.

A similar proof can be derived for the case where we have out-anchors for each factor and columns of QQ are rr-disjunct. ∎

We suspect that an identifiability theorem can be derived from these weaker conditions and leave it for future work.

=FX​({ρZ​(ρZ−1​(FZ​(𝐱PaZ)))}Z∈PaX,𝐮)\displaystyle=F_{X}\left(\{\rho_{Z}(\rho_{Z}^{-1}(F_{Z}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{Z}})))\}_{Z\in\mathrm{Pa}_{X}},\mathbf{u}\right)
