where r=(rX)X∈𝒳r=(r_{X})_{X\in\mathcal{X}} and δ=(δZ)Z∈𝒵\delta=(\delta_{Z})_{Z\in\mathcal{Z}}.

Expectation and nilpotency.

Taking 𝔼i∼ℙ𝐮∼P​r\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\sim\mathbb{P}\\ \mathbf{u}\sim\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits\end{subarray}} preserves the componentwise inequality, giving

D≤M​R+(M​N)​D,D\leq MR+(MN)D,

where DZ:=𝔼⁡[δZ]D_{Z}:=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{Z}] and RX:=𝔼⁡[rX]R_{X}:=\mathbb{E}[r_{X}].

Because the underlying f-DAG is acyclic, the induced factor-level graph is acyclic, by Lemma 10.

The matrix M​NMN has support contained in this adjacency, hence is nilpotent: (M​N)γ=0(MN)^{\gamma}=0 for some γ≤|𝒵|=m\gamma\leq|\mathcal{Z}|=m. Therefore

(I−M​N)−1=∑k=0γ−1(M​N)k(I-MN)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\gamma-1}(MN)^{k}

is well-defined and entrywise nonnegative.

Left-multiplying (I−M​N)​D≤M​R(I-MN)D\leq MR by (I−M​N)−1≥0(I-MN)^{-1}\geq 0 preserves the order:

D\displaystyle D ≤(I−M​N)−1​M​R\displaystyle\leq(I-MN)^{-1}MR
=∑k=0γ−1(M​N)k​M​R\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{\gamma-1}(MN)^{k}MR

Summing coordinates and using any submultiplicative norm (e.g. ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1}) yields

Δ^\displaystyle\hat{\Delta} =𝔼⁡[∑Z∈𝒵δZ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{Z}}\delta_{Z}\right]
=‖D‖1\displaystyle=\|D\|_{1}
≤(‖M‖1​∑k=0γ−1‖M​N‖1k)⋅‖R‖1\displaystyle\leq\Bigl(\|M\|_{1}\sum_{k=0}^{\gamma-1}\|MN\|_{1}^{k}\Bigr)\cdot\|R\|_{1}

Relating ‖R‖1\|R\|_{1} to the score S⁡(Φ,Θ)S(\Phi,\Theta).

Under the Gaussian conditional model used for pΘXp_{\Theta}^{X} (with variance σX2\sigma_{X}^{2}),

log⁡pΘX​(𝐱X∣𝐳^PaX)=−12​σX2​‖𝐱X−x^X‖2−cX,cX:=12​log⁡(2​π​σX2),\log p_{\Theta}^{X}(\mathbf{x}_{X}\mid\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{Pa}_{X}})=-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{X}^{2}}\|\mathbf{x}_{X}-\hat{x}_{X}\|^{2}-c_{X},\qquad c_{X}:=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_{X}^{2}),

hence, taking 𝔼i∼ℙ𝐮∼P​r\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\sim\mathbb{P}\\ \mathbf{u}\sim\mathop{\mathrm{P}r}\nolimits\end{subarray}} and summing over X∉𝐈X\notin\mathbf{I},

S(Φ,Θ)=−∑X∈𝒳12​σX2RX−C0,C0:=𝔼i∼ℙ[∑X∉𝐈cX].\displaystyle S(\Phi,\Theta)=-\sum_{X\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{2\sigma_{X}^{2}}R_{X}-C_{0},\qquad C_{0}:=\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathbb{P}}\Big[\sum_{X\notin\mathbf{I}}c_{X}\Big].

Let σmax2:=maxX⁡σX2\sigma_{\max}^{2}:=\max_{X}\sigma_{X}^{2}. Then

‖R‖1\displaystyle\|R\|_{1} =∑XRX\displaystyle=\sum_{X}R_{X}
≤2​σmax2​∑X12​σX2​RX\displaystyle\leq 2\sigma_{\max}^{2}\sum_{X}\frac{1}{2\sigma_{X}^{2}}R_{X}
=2​σmax2​(−S⁡(Φ,Θ)−C0)\displaystyle=2\sigma_{\max}^{2}\bigl(-S(\Phi,\Theta)-C_{0}\bigr)

Combining with the previous bound on Δ^\hat{\Delta} gives

Δ^≤2​σmax2​‖M‖1​∑k=0γ−1‖M​N‖1k​(−S⁡(Φ,Θ)−C0),\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}\leq 2\sigma_{\max}^{2}\ \|M\|_{1}\sum_{k=0}^{\gamma-1}\|MN\|_{1}^{k}\ \bigl(-S(\Phi,\Theta)-C_{0}\bigr),

which is an affine bound in S⁡(Φ,Θ)S(\Phi,\Theta). ∎

Appendix C Practical implementation details

C.1 Acyclicity constraint formulations

We implement the main differentiable formulations for acyclicity constraints, all of the form h⁡(A)=0⇔Gh(A)=0\iff G is a DAG. We consider A∈ℝ+n×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{+}, for which nilpotence is equivalent to DAGness of GG.

Matrix exponential (tr-exp). Introduced by Zheng et al. [2018], this formulation defines:

hexp​(A)=tr⁡(eA)−nh_{\text{exp}}(A)=\tr\bigl(e^{A}\bigr)-n

where AA is the (possibly weighted) n×nn\times n adjacency matrix. Computing eAe^{A} costs O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}).

Matrix power. This formulation uses:

hpow​(A)=tr⁡[(I+An)n]−nh_{\text{pow}}(A)=\tr\left[\left(I+\frac{A}{n}\right)^{n}\right]-n

which avoids the matrix exponential but retains the same O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) cost due to the matrix power computation.

Spectral radius. Proposed by [Lee et al., 2019], the spectral radius formulation enforces:

hρ​(A)=ρ​(A)h_{\rho}(A)=\rho\bigl(A\bigr)

where ρ⁡(⋅)\rho(\cdot) is the spectral radius (largest eigenvalue in modulus). The spectral radius is computed via power iteration with TT steps, costing O⁡(T​n2)O(Tn^{2}) per gradient step. Nazaret et al. [2024] showed that this formulation is numerically more stable than the tr-exp and matrix power approaches, which we experimentally verify.

Reduction to the factor graph. Since A=Q⋄R⊤A=Q\diamond R^{\top} is a rank-mm Boolean matrix with m<nm<n, a key structural property allows working with the much smaller m×mm\times m factor adjacency:

Lemma 10 (Lopez et al. [2022]).

GG is acyclic ⇔\iff GXG_{X} is acyclic ⇔\iff GZG_{Z} is acyclic.

Consequently, any of the above formulations can be applied to the factor adjacency B=R⊤⋄Q∈ℝ+m×mB=R^{\top}\diamond Q\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}_{+} instead of the full variable adjacency A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. This reduces the tr-exp and matrix power costs from O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) to O⁡(m3+n​m2)O(m^{3}+nm^{2}), and the spectral radius cost from O⁡(T​n2)O(Tn^{2}) to O⁡(T​m2+n​m2)O(Tm^{2}+nm^{2}), with memory dropping from O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) to O⁡(m2)O(m^{2}).

Spectral radius adapted for the bipartite structure. Lopez et al. [2022] further exploit the bipartite structure to avoid forming BB altogether. The bipartite adjacency can be written as the block matrix:

M=(0QR⊤0)∈ℝ+(n+m)×(n+m)M=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q\\ R^{\top}&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+m)\times(n+m)}_{+}

Power iteration on MM decomposes into alternating matrix-vector products with QQ and R⊤R^{\top}:

  1. 1.

    Initialize left and right eigenvector buffers xv∈ℝn,xf∈ℝm,yv∈ℝn,yf∈ℝmx_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},x_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},y_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},y_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.

  2. 2.

    For t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T: normalize xf←R⊤​xv/‖R⊤​xv‖x_{f}\leftarrow R^{\top}x_{v}/\|R^{\top}x_{v}\|, then xv←Q​xf/‖Q​xf‖x_{v}\leftarrow Q\,x_{f}/\|Q\,x_{f}\|; symmetrically for yy.

  3. 3.

    Compute the spectral radius estimate via the gradient formula:

    ρ=yv⊤​Q​xf+yf⊤​R⊤​xvyf⊤​xf+yv⊤​xv\rho=\frac{y_{v}^{\top}Q\,x_{f}+y_{f}^{\top}R^{\top}x_{v}}{y_{f}^{\top}x_{f}+y_{v}^{\top}x_{v}}

    with ∇Qρ=yv​xf⊤yf⊤​xf+yv⊤​xv\nabla_{Q}\rho=\frac{y_{v}x_{f}^{\top}}{y_{f}^{\top}x_{f}+y_{v}^{\top}x_{v}} and ∇Rρ=xv​yf⊤yf⊤​xf+yv⊤​xv\nabla_{R}\rho=\frac{x_{v}y_{f}^{\top}}{y_{f}^{\top}x_{f}+y_{v}^{\top}x_{v}}.

Each iteration costs O⁡(n​m)O(nm), yielding a total of O⁡(T​n​m)O(Tnm) per gradient step with O⁡(n​m)O(nm) memory, never forming any n×nn\times n or m×mm\times m matrix. The complexity of all approaches is summarized in Table 3.

In practice, in accordance with the insights of Nazaret et al. [2024], we observed that spectral radius methods are less prone to numerical instabilities than other formulation. In particular, we found the bipartite spectral radius formulation to be the most stable and efficient, and is used in all our experiments on non-layered DAGs.

Layered DAG constraint. When variables X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} are organized into LL known layers (e.g., neurons in successive layers of a neural network), we can replace the general acyclicity constraint with a cheap structural constraint that also enforces this ordering constraint. Let ℓ⁡(i)∈{0,…,L−1}\ell(i)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\} denote the layer of variable ii. For the graph to be acyclic, it suffices that every factor has all its parents in strictly earlier layers than all its children:

∀k∈[m],maxi:Qi​k=1ℓ(i)<minj:Rj​k=1ℓ(j).\forall k\in[m],\quad\max_{i:Q_{ik}=1}\ell(i)<\min_{j:R_{jk}=1}\ell(j).

To make this differentiable, we aggregate the relaxed assignment matrices Q,R∈(0,1)n×mQ,R\in(0,1)^{n\times m} into per-layer masses for each factor kk:

qk​l:=∑i:ℓ⁡(i)=lQi​k,rk​l:=∑j:ℓ⁡(j)=lRj​k.q_{kl}:=\sum_{i:\ell(i)=l}Q_{ik},\qquad r_{kl}:=\sum_{j:\ell(j)=l}R_{jk}.

This aggregation is computed in O⁡(n​m)O(nm) time. We then compute for each factor kk a violation score that measures the total mass of parent-child pairs violating the layer ordering:

bk:=∑lp≥lcqk,lp⋅rk,lc.b_{k}:=\sum_{l_{p}\geq l_{c}}q_{k,l_{p}}\cdot r_{k,l_{c}}.

This is evaluated efficiently using a cumulative sum: letting r¯k,l:=∑l′≤lrk,l′\bar{r}_{k,l}:=\sum_{l^{\prime}\leq l}r_{k,l^{\prime}}, we obtain bk=∑l=0L−1qk,l⋅r¯k,lb_{k}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}q_{k,l}\cdot\bar{r}_{k,l} in O⁡(m​L)O(mL) time. In the binary case, bk=0b_{k}=0 is equivalent to the strict layer ordering; in the relaxed case, bkb_{k} continuously measures the degree of violation.

For scale stability, we optionally normalize by the total mass:

b¯k:=bk(∑lqk​l)​(∑lrk​l)+ϵ.\bar{b}_{k}:=\frac{b_{k}}{\left(\sum_{l}q_{kl}\right)\left(\sum_{l}r_{kl}\right)+\epsilon}.

The constraint is formulated as the inequality b¯k−ε≤0\bar{b}_{k}-\varepsilon\leq 0 for each factor kk, with tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0. The total cost is O⁡(n​m+m​L)O(nm+mL), i.e. O⁡(n​m)O(nm) since L≤nL\leq n.

C.2 Causal graph sampling

During training, the graph G⁡(Φ)G(\Phi) is sampled stochastically at each forward pass. We parameterize the bipartite structure through a single logit tensor W⁡(Φ)∈ℝn×m×3W(\Phi)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m\times 3}, where for each variable-factor pair (i,k)(i,k) the three categories encode: 0 for a parent edge (Qi​k=1Q_{ik}=1, i.e., variable ii is a parent of factor kk), 1 for child edge (Ri​k=1R_{ik}=1, i.e., variable ii is a child of factor kk), and 2 for no edge. Sampling is performed with the Gumbel-softmax trick [Jang et al., 2017, Maddison et al., 2017], using straight-through hard samples for the forward pass while allowing gradients to flow through the soft relaxation.

C.3 Anchor constraint

Recall that Assumption 4 requires each factor ZZ with index k∈[m]k\in[m] to have at least one in-anchor and one out-anchor. We formalize this as a differentiable constraint.

For in-anchors, the score measuring how exclusively variable ii is assigned to factor kk as a parent is:

si→kin=Qi​k​∏ℓ≠k(1−Qi​ℓ).s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}=Q_{ik}\prod_{\ell\neq k}(1-Q_{i\ell}).

The in-anchor count for factor kk is then ckin=∑i=1nsi→kinc^{\text{in}}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}, and symmetrically ckout=∑j=1nsj→koutc^{\text{out}}_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}s^{\text{out}}_{j\to k} for out-anchors computed on RR.

To avoid numerical underflow from the product of many terms close to 1, we compute the scores in log-space using the log-sum-exp decomposition:

Si:=∑ℓ=1mlog⁡(1−Qi​ℓ+ϵ),log⁡si→kin=log⁡(Qi​k+ϵ)+Si−log⁡(1−Qi​k+ϵ),S_{i}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\log(1-Q_{i\ell}+\epsilon),\qquad\log s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}=\log(Q_{ik}+\epsilon)+S_{i}-\log(1-Q_{ik}+\epsilon),

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a small constant for numerical stability. SiS_{i} is the total log-complement sum across all factors, and subtracting the kk-th term gives the product over ℓ≠k\ell\neq k without an explicit loop. The anchor score is recovered as si→kin=exp⁡(log⁡si→kin)s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}=\exp(\log s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}), and the count is ckin=∑isi→kinc^{\text{in}}_{k}=\sum_{i}s^{\text{in}}_{i\to k}.

This computation runs in O⁡(n​m)O(nm) time for all factors simultaneously. The constraint is formulated as:

𝒞anchor​(Φ):=∑k=1m[max⁡(τ−ckin,0)+max⁡(τ−ckout,0)]\mathcal{C}^{\text{anchor}}(\Phi):=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\left[\max\bigl(\tau-c^{\text{in}}_{k},0\bigr)+\max\bigl(\tau-c^{\text{out}}_{k},0\bigr)\right]

where τ≤1\tau\leq 1 is a threshold (we use τ=0.99\tau=0.99). In practice, we impose per-factor inequality constraints τ−ckin≤0\tau-c^{\text{in}}_{k}\leq 0 and τ−ckout≤0\tau-c^{\text{out}}_{k}\leq 0 within the Augmented Lagrangian framework.

Appendix D Experiments

D.1 Implementation details

Our implementation heavily modifies the open source implementation of Lopez et al. [2022], in particular in the way we solve the constrained optimization problem. Our model is implemented in PyTorch [Ansel et al., 2024]. Constrained optimization is handled by Cooper [Gallego-Posada et al., 2025], which provides an Augmented Lagrangian framework for differentiable constraints.

Training loop. At each epoch, the model iterates over mini-batches of observational and interventional data. For each batch (𝐱,mask,regime)(\mathbf{x},\text{mask},\text{regime}):

  1. 1.

    A graph G′G^{\prime} is sampled via Gumbel-softmax from the tensor W⁡(Φ)W(\Phi).

  2. 2.

    The model computes predictions 𝐱^\hat{\mathbf{x}} by passing inputs through the sampled factor graph (variables →\to factors via FZΘF_{Z}^{\Theta}, then factors →\to variables via FXΘF_{X}^{\Theta}).

  3. 3.

    The data-fitting loss (negative log-likelihood) is computed over non-intervened variables.

  4. 4.

    Constraint violations (DAG or layer ordering, anchors, L1L_{1} sparsity) are evaluated.

  5. 5.

    Cooper’s Augmented Lagrangian solver performs alternating primal-dual updates: the primal optimizer (Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2014]) minimizes the Lagrangian, while the dual optimizer (SGD) updates the Lagrange multipliers.

Constrained optimization. All constraints use an Augmented Lagrangian formulation with inequality constraints 𝒞⁡(Φ)≤0\mathcal{C}(\Phi)\leq 0.

Hyperparameters. The primal learning rate is selected from {2×10−4,5×10−4,7×10−4,1×10−3,2×10−3}\{2\times 10^{-4},5\times 10^{-4},7\times 10^{-4},1\times 10^{-3},2\times 10^{-3}\} depending on the setting. The dual learning rate is set as 15\frac{1}{5} of the primal rate. The penalty coefficient ρc\rho_{c} is grown at a multiplicative rate of 1.0031.003 or 1.0041.004 per epoch. Batch size is 512512 and training runs for up to 50 00050\,000 epochs with early stopping: patience of 20002000 epochs begins once all active constraints are satisfied. The L1L_{1} sparsity tolerance is set to tols=0.2\text{tol}_{s}=0.2.

Post-processing. After training, the continuous logits W⁡(Φ)W(\Phi) are discretized: for each variable-factor pair, we apply softmax over the three categories and assign the argmax direction (parent, child, or no edge), subject to a minimum confidence threshold on the total edge probability. Acyclicity of the recovered graph is then verified.

Model selection and evaluation. For each experimental setting, we run a grid of hyperparameters (learning rate, penalty growth) over multiple random seeds and DAG instances. Model selection is performed on a validation set: among all runs that reach feasibility (all constraints satisfied), we select the one with the lowest validation negative log-likelihood. Test metrics are then computed on held-out observational data from the same DAG.

D.2 Metrics

We evaluate the quality of the learned causal abstraction by measuring factor recovery. Since factors are identifiable only up to reparameterization, we evaluate whether the learned factors 𝐳^=τ^​(𝐱)\hat{\mathbf{z}}=\hat{\tau}(\mathbf{x}) align with the ground-truth factors 𝐳\mathbf{z}, using metrics invariant to the admissible symmetry class.

  • •

    Mean correlation coefficient (MCC): finds the permutation alignment with highest absolute correlation between 𝐳\mathbf{z} and 𝐳^\hat{\mathbf{z}} averaged over all factors. We report MCC with Pearson correlation (invariant to component-wise affine transformations), Spearman rank correlation (invariant to component-wise monotone transformations), and the Randomized Dependence Coefficient (RDC, Lopez-Paz et al. [2013], invariant to component-wise nonlinear transformations).

  • •

    Explicitness (R2R^{2}): for each ground-truth factor, we fit a linear regression (or a small MLP) from all learned factors and report the variance-explained R2R^{2}, averaged over factors. R2R^{2}-linear measures linear decodability; R2R^{2}-MLP measures nonlinear decodability. Contrary to MCC which is sensitive to linear mixing by a matrix, R2R^{2} is not.

  • •

    Disentanglement, Completeness, Informativeness (DCI) [Eastwood and Williams, 2018]: fits gradient boosted trees from learned factors to each ground-truth factor, extracts feature importances, and computes entropy-based scores. Disentanglement measures whether each learned dimension captures at most one ground-truth factor; Completeness measures whether each ground-truth factor is captured by at most one learned dimension; Informativeness is the predictive R2R^{2}.

D.3 Synthetic experiments

Data generation. We generate synthetic f-SCMs by first sampling a random bipartite DAG GG over nn variables and mm factors. Edge probabilities are set so that the graph is moderately sparse (probability of an edge set to 0.10.1). When anchors are desired, the graph generator enforces Assumption 4 by checking whether they are verified, otherwise the graph is resampled. When variables are organized into layers, factors are constrained to have parents in strictly earlier layers than children.

For each DAG, variable-to-factor mechanisms FZF_{Z} are either linear (weights drawn uniformly from [±0.25,±1][\pm 0.25,\pm 1]) or nonlinear (two-layer neural networks with tanh\tanh activation and standard normal weights, i.e., each weight drawn i.i.d. from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)). Factor-to-variable mechanisms FXF_{X} follow the same scheme. When the setting is noiseless, factors and variables are computed deterministically; otherwise, additive Gaussian noise with scale 0.40.4 is added to variables (factors remain noiseless).

Data are generated under hard stochastic interventions: a certain amount of interventional regimes target 11 to33 variables each, plus one observational regime. Each dataset contains n=10 000n=10\,000 samples. We generate 55 independent DAG instances per setting to account for graph variability.

Evaluation. We evaluate UCAD across settings of variable difficulty (all with continuous variables and enforced anchors). We sweep across a few learning rates, dual learning rate, penalty multiplier, and seeds. In the following tables, the DAGness constraint violation may be negative because we target 𝒞DAG≤10−6\mathcal{C}^{\text{DAG}}\leq 10^{-6}, and anything respecting the constraint will have a negative violation.

(a) Linear noiseless, layered (n∈{16,64,128}n\in\{16,64,128\}, m∈{3,6,8}m\in\{3,6,8\}, L=3L=3 layers). Both FZF_{Z} and FXF_{X} are linear, no noise is added to the variables, and variables are organized into layers (e.g., [4,8,4][4,8,4] for n=16n=16).

(b) Linear noiseless, not layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}). Same as (a) but without layer structure. We employ the spectral radius DAG constraint adapted for Q⋄R⊤Q\diamond R^{\top}.

(c) Nonlinear FZF_{Z}, noiseless, layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}, L=3L=3 layers). The learned model uses a 2-layer MLP for FZΘF_{Z}^{\Theta} while FXΘF_{X}^{\Theta} remains linear. No noise is added to variables.

(d) Nonlinear FZF_{Z}, noiseless, not layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}). Same as (c) but without layer structure.

(e) Nonlinear FZF_{Z}, noisy, not layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}). Same as (d) but with additive Gaussian noise (scale 0.40.4) on variables.

(f) Nonlinear FXF_{X}, noisy, not layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}). The learned model uses a 2-layer MLP for FXΘF_{X}^{\Theta} while FZΘF_{Z}^{\Theta} remains linear.

(g) Both FZ,FXF_{Z},F_{X} nonlinear, noisy, not layered (n∈{16,64}n\in\{16,64\}, m∈{3,6}m\in\{3,6\}). Both FZF_{Z} and FXF_{X} are nonlinear MLPs. The learned model uses 2-layer MLPs for both FZΘF_{Z}^{\Theta} and FXΘF_{X}^{\Theta} (hidden dim 1616).

In the case where we expect the f-SCM to be recoverable up to linear reparametrization (i.e., when FXF_{X} and/or FZF_{Z} are affine), a perfect MCC-Pearson of 11 is theoretically attainable. We observe that the performance of our model is fairly invariant to the number of variables (16,6416,64 or 128128) and factors (3,63,6 or 88), to whether the DAG has a layered structure or not, and to whether additive Gaussian noise is added on the variables. When averaging over all these cases (13 experiments) we measure an average MCC (Pearson) of 0.830.83. Importantly, the variability we observe between all cases does not seem to depend on whether both FX,FZF_{X},F_{Z} are linear or only one of them.

In the case where both FX,FZF_{X},F_{Z} are non-linear, we can only recover the factors up to an arbitrary bijective transformation, which results in a drop of MCC-Pearson. The MCC-RDC score remains high, at 0.790.79 in the 64 variables case, and 0.700.70 in the 16 variables case. We note however that DCI metrics and R2R^{2}-MLP, which are also metrics that should not be sensitive to non-linear transformations, are not matching this trend. Since the variance of MCC-RDC remains low, it does not look like a seed artefact, and experiments on more graphs are needed to understand where this discrepancy comes from.

Ablations.

We report additional experiments.

(h) Both FZ,FXF_{Z},F_{X} are linear, noiseless, not layered (n=64n=64, m=6m=6). The model is trained only on the observational regime, and tested on held-out observational samples.

We observe performances similar to the case where the model is also trained on interventional regimes. This setting may be simple, but still clearly hints at a good robustness of the model when only trained on observational data.

(i) Both FZ,FXF_{Z},F_{X} are linear, noiseless, not layered (n=64n=64, m=6m=6). The model is trained on a subset of interventional regimes and tested on new ones. Following the code of Lopez et al. [2022], each interventional regime has a fixed target set of 1 to 3 observed variables. Targeted variables are replaced by a new Normal​(0,1)\text{Normal}(0,1) draw, and non-target variables are simulated by the equations of the f-SCM. In total, 64 interventional regimes are created. Training samples are generated by the observational regime and 46 interventional regimes, validation is computed on 6 separate regimes, while test metrics are computed on 12 separate regimes.

We observe performances similar to the case where the model is tested on held-out observational regimes. This setting may be simple, but still clearly hints at a good robustness of the abstractions when tested on new interventional regimes.

D.4 Interpretability

We consider the problem of classifying whether an integer n∈{0,…,999,999}n\in\{0,\dots,999,999\} is divisible by 66. The input is the base-1010 representation (d0,…,dK−1)∈{0,…,9}K(d_{0},\dots,d_{K-1})\in\{0,\dots,9\}^{K} with K=6K=6 digits (from ones to hundred-thousands), and the label is y=𝟏​[6∣n]∈{0,1}y=\mathbf{1}[6\mid n]\in\{0,1\}. Each digit dkd_{k} is encoded as a 1010-dimensional one-hot vector, giving an input dimension of K×10=60K\times 10=60.

We train a fully-connected MLP with architecture [60,32,32,32,1][60,32,32,32,1]: three hidden layers of 3232 neurons with ReLU activations, followed by a single output logit trained with binary cross-entropy loss. Training uses the Adam optimizer (learning rate 10−310^{-3}, batch size 128128) with early stopping (patience 2525, up to 200200 epochs) on an 80/2080/20 train/test split of all 10610^{6} integers. The network reaches an almost perfect test accuracy.

We view the trained MLP as a low-level SCM ℒ\mathcal{L} whose endogenous variables 𝒳\mathcal{X} are the post-ReLU activations of all hidden neurons, giving n=|𝒳|=32+32+32=96n=|\mathcal{X}|=32+32+32=96 variables. The causal graph GLG_{L} of ℒ\mathcal{L} is determined by the network connectivity: every neuron in hidden layer ℓ\ell is a parent of every neuron in hidden layer ℓ+1\ell+1 (and the last hidden layer feeds into the logit), forming a strictly layered DAG with layer sizes [32,32,32][32,32,32]. The mechanisms ℱL\mathcal{F}_{L} are the trained affine maps composed with ReLU (or identity for the logit), and the context 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L} corresponds to the input nn (encoded as one-hot). Since the network is deterministic, the context (here, the input of the network) fully determines all activations.

To collect interventional data, we perform hard interventions on each of the 9696 hidden neurons individually (excluding the output logit). For each neuron XjX_{j} in hidden layer ℓ\ell, we clamp its post-ReLU activation to a value resampled from its empirical training distribution and record the resulting activations of all downstream neurons. Concretely, for a subsample of 500500 inputs per intervention, we perform a forward pass where XjX_{j} is replaced by a draw from its marginal: Xj←x~jX_{j}\leftarrow\tilde{x}_{j}, with x~j\tilde{x}_{j} sampled uniformly from the training-set values of XjX_{j}. This yields 96×500=48,00096\times 500=48,000 interventional samples, combined with 200,000200,000 observational samples (test-set forward passes) for a total of 248,000248,000 samples.

Among the 248,000248,000 samples, 80% are used to train UCAD, and 20% are used for validation and model selection. We build a separate held-out observational set of 1,0001,000 samples for test, on which we report the metrics below.

When applying UCAD we search over m∈{2,3}m\in\{2,3\} factors, and select the model with the lowest validation NLL among runs that achieved constraint feasibility (DAG, anchor, and sparsity constraints). We evaluate the learned factors against positive concepts: c2=𝟏​[2∣n]c_{2}=\mathbf{1}[2\mid n], c3=𝟏​[3∣n]c_{3}=\mathbf{1}[3\mid n], c6=𝟏​[6∣n]c_{6}=\mathbf{1}[6\mid n], and c~3=∑kdk\tilde{c}_{3}=\sum_{k}d_{k} (the sum of all digits, an intermediate quantity involved in the intuitive computation of divisibility by 33); and negative controls: 𝟏​[5∣n]\mathbf{1}[5\mid n], 𝟏​[7∣n]\mathbf{1}[7\mid n], 𝟏​[11∣n]\mathbf{1}[11\mid n]. Results are reported in Table 14 below.

We measure a stronger reconstruction of hypothesized concepts than with negative controls (average MCC-RDC of 0.720.72 vs. 0.070.07 over 5 experiments). In particular, one of the factors has an average Pearson correlation of 0.800.80 with c2c_{2}, which is a strong signal that it is consistently implemented by the network. Reasonably high MCC-RDC coefficients can be observed for c6c_{6} and c3c_{3}, especially compared to negative controls which are not reconstructed as well. Interestingly, the negative control c5c_{5} is reconstructed by one of the factors as much as the sum of all digits c~3\tilde{c}_{3} (average MCC-RDC of 0.140.14 vs. 0.160.16).

These results remain difficult to interpret, keeping in mind that our intuitive method to compute c3c_{3} is recursive. Furthermore, a low agreement with some concept may not necessarily indicate a failure of UCAD, but could simply mean that the DNN implements a different strategy to solve the problem, for example a heuristic that works only up to 1 million that might sometimes rely on divisibility by 55 for some reason. This illustrates the difficulty of validating such a method: we look for tasks where we expect the DNN to implement a given logic, but our method might unveil that the network implements a different algorithm compared to what was expected. Thus, more work is required to interpret the factors that were learned.
